triage.name: Pancreatitis
triage.reason: Classic acute abdomen with epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea and elevated lipase; strong differential and management decisions.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast' was in confirmatory, not_indicated; kept confirmatory as a conditional order (only if Severe disease, diagnostic uncertainty, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours)
auto-repaired: workup: 'tg' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Lipemic serum, no gallstones or alcohol use, or known elevated triglycerides)

auto-repaired: workup: 'MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography)' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Suspected choledocholithiasis not confirmed by ultrasound)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Chest x-ray' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Dyspnea, hypoxia, or suspected respiratory complication)

demographics: Gallstone pancreatitis is more common in women, especially after age 50
Alcohol-related pancreatitis is more common in men

chief_complaints.text: I have severe pain in the upper part of my stomach
The pain goes straight through to my back

hpi.onset: Sudden, often over one to two hours; may begin after a large meal or alcohol binge
hpi.duration: Usually less than 48 hours at presentation
hpi.progression: Pain rapidly reaches maximum intensity and becomes constant; vomiting may follow the onset of pain.
hpi.radiation: Straight through to the back or left flank
pertinent_negatives: Chest pain radiating to the left arm

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Pleuritic chest pain with cough and fever
Sudden one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with vague abdominal pain, irritability and vomiting; they may not describe radiation to the back.
Older adults may have less severe pain and less fever; they may present with hypotension, confusion or malaise rather than typical epigastric pain.
Pregnancy increases the risk of gallstone pancreatitis; pain can be attributed to pregnancy or gallbladder disease, and the gravid uterus may modify exam findings.

general.mild: Uncomfortable but appears well; may be restless, leaning forward
general.moderate: Moderate distress; lying still or leaning forward, may be diaphoretic
general.severe: Severe distress; pale, diaphoretic, anxious; may have tachypnea
general.critical: Toxic-appearing; obtunded or somnolent; signs of shock (cool, mottled, hypotensive)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the epigastrium and left upper quadrant, starting away from the point of maximal pain

findings.finding: Voluntary guarding in the upper abdomen

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough or gently percuss the abdomen; avoid deep palpation if guarding
findings.finding: Pain with coughing or gentle percussion

findings.maneuver: Perform pelvic exam when a gynecologic cause is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness or adnexal mass

labs.caveat: A lipase above three times the upper limit of normal is strongly supportive; the height does not reliably predict severity.
Less sensitive than lipase; may be normal in alcohol-related pancreatitis and elevated in many non-pancreatic conditions.
A CRP above 15 mg/dL at 48 hours suggests severe pancreatitis, but early values are less helpful.
Elevated BUN reflects volume depletion and is part of severity scoring.
Acute kidney injury complicates severe pancreatitis.
Hyperglycemia occurs from pancreatic endocrine dysfunction and stress.
Hypocalcemia in severe pancreatitis reflects fat saponification and is a poor prognostic sign.
Elevated lactate suggests tissue hypoperfusion or necrosis.
Elevation suggests a gallstone or bile duct obstruction as the cause.
A marked early AST rise can suggest gallstone pancreatitis.
Often rises with hepatocellular injury from gallstone pancreatitis.
Often rises with bile duct obstruction.
A level above 1000 mg/dL can cause pancreatitis and requires specific treatment.
Negative in pancreatitis. Always check in any woman who could be pregnant before imaging and to rule out ectopic pregnancy.

findings.finding: No ST-segment elevation or reciprocal changes

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Severe or worsening pancreatitis, suspected necrosis, or diagnostic uncertainty

findings.text: Diffuse or focal pancreatic enlargement with peripancreatic fat stranding

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the right upper quadrant
imaging.preferred_when: Initial evaluation for gallstone etiology, pregnancy, or when avoiding radiation
Suspected common bile duct stone not seen on ultrasound, or pregnancy when ultrasound inconclusive

findings.text: Common bile duct stone or gallstones
Dilated biliary tree without visible stone
Nonspecific; sentinel loop of dilated small bowel or colon cutoff sign

initial.why: Leukocytosis and hemoconcentration help assess inflammation and fluid status.
Evaluates electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, and calcium; derangements are common and prognostically important.
Elevated lipase is the preferred enzyme for diagnosis.
Liver enzymes and bilirubin identify a biliary cause.
Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before imaging.

initial.test: Ultrasound of the right upper quadrant
initial.why: Looks for gallstones and bile duct dilation as the cause.

confirmatory.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Confirms diagnosis when classic features are not present and identifies complications such as necrosis, abscess, or fluid collections.
confirmatory.only_if: Severe disease, diagnostic uncertainty, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours

supporting.why: A high CRP at 48 hours suggests severe disease.
Elevation suggests tissue hypoperfusion and severe disease.
Identifies hypertriglyceridemia as a treatable cause.
supporting.only_if: Lipemic serum, no gallstones or alcohol use, or known elevated triglycerides

supporting.why: Noninvasive way to look for a common bile duct stone when ultrasound is inconclusive.
supporting.only_if: Suspected choledocholithiasis not confirmed by ultrasound

supporting.why: Evaluates for ARDS, pleural effusion, or other pulmonary complications.
supporting.only_if: Dyspnea, hypoxia, or suspected respiratory complication

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management and is nonspecific.
No role in the evaluation of pancreatitis.

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant.
Ultrasound first to look for gallstones; CT is reserved for severe, uncertain, or non-improving cases.
Do not delay fluid resuscitation and supportive care for imaging.
For suspected common bile duct stone, consider early ERCP if cholangitis or persistent obstruction.

criteria.name: Revised Atlanta criteria for acute pancreatitis (diagnosis)
criteria.summary: Acute pancreatitis requires at least two of three features.
items: Serum lipase or amylase at least three times the upper limit of normal
Imaging findings consistent with acute pancreatitis

differential.name: Acute cholangitis
differential.why_considered: Fever, jaundice, and upper abdominal pain can overlap with gallstone pancreatitis
differential.trigger: Charcot triad of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain

history: Older age or known gallstones
Fever and rigors
Pain may be less severe than pancreatitis but jaundice is prominent
exam: Hypotension or altered mental status in severe cholangitis
labs: Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin
Lipase may be normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: Bile duct dilation on ultrasound or CT
Stone or pus in the common bile duct on MRCP or ERCP

differential.name: Perforated peptic ulcer
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe epigastric pain and peritonitis can mimic severe pancreatitis
differential.trigger: Sudden onset of severe epigastric pain with a rigid abdomen

history: History of NSAID use, Helicobacter pylori infection, or prior ulcer
Pain may begin suddenly and then spread across the abdomen
Nausea and vomiting may follow pain, similar to pancreatitis
labs: Lipase usually normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: Free intraperitoneal air on upright chest x-ray or CT

differential.name: Acute myocardial infarction
differential.why_considered: Epigastric discomfort, nausea, and diaphoresis can be the presenting symptoms of an inferior MI
differential.trigger: Cardiac risk factors and epigastric discomfort with diaphoresis or dyspnea

history: Chest pressure or burning that may radiate to the jaw, neck, or left arm
Shortness of breath
Nausea and vomiting
Prior cardiac disease or risk factors
exam: Signs of heart failure such as crackles or elevated JVP
ecg: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF
Reciprocal ST depression in lateral leads

differential.name: Mesenteric ischemia
differential.why_considered: Severe epigastric or periumbilical pain with relative absence of early tenderness can mimic pancreatitis
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to exam in an older patient with atrial fibrillation or vascular disease

history: Atrial fibrillation, heart failure, or atherosclerotic disease
Sudden severe pain out of proportion to abdominal exam
Nausea and vomiting
exam: Early: mild or no tenderness despite severe pain
labs: Lipase usually normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: CT angiography showing superior mesenteric artery occlusion or bowel wall thickening/pneumatosis

differential.name: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
differential.why_considered: Epigastric or back pain with hypotension can mimic severe pancreatitis
differential.trigger: Older patient with abdominal or back pain and hypotension or a pulsatile mass

history: Known AAA or vascular risk factors
Sudden tearing pain in abdomen, back, or flank
Syncope or near-syncope
exam: Mottled or cool extremities if exsanguinating
imaging: CT angiography shows a ruptured AAA with retroperitoneal hematoma

differential.name: Acute cholecystitis
differential.why_considered: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain after eating with nausea can resemble gallstone pancreatitis

history: Pain more localized to the right upper quadrant
Pain often radiates to right shoulder or scapula
Prior biliary colic attacks
exam: Right upper quadrant tenderness without epigastric predominance
labs: Lipase normal or only mildly elevated
AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase may be elevated
imaging: Gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and gallstones on ultrasound

history: Vomiting and diarrhea often begin before pain
Watery diarrhea
Sick contacts

severity.mild: Interstitial edematous pancreatitis with no organ failure or local complications; pain is manageable and vital signs are stable.
severity.moderate: Transient organ failure that resolves within 48 hours or local complications such as peripancreatic fluid collections; more marked SIRS.
severity.severe: Persistent organ failure lasting more than 48 hours, infected necrosis, or other major local complications; often requires intensive care.
severity.critical: Multiple organ dysfunction, shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or infected pancreatic necrosis with sepsis; life-threatening.

red_flags.finding: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg or persistent tachycardia
red_flags.meaning: Third-spacing and hypovolemic shock; needs aggressive fluid resuscitation and ICU.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome or large pleural effusion.
Sepsis, hypoperfusion, or pancreatic encephalopathy; severe disease.
Perforation, hemorrhagic pancreatitis, or other surgical emergency.
Hemorrhagic pancreatitis with retroperitoneal bleeding; poor prognosis.

red_flags.finding: Persistent fever after the first week
red_flags.meaning: Infected pancreatic necrosis until proven otherwise.
Acute kidney injury and severe pancreatitis.

complications.name: Acute peripancreatic fluid collection
clues: CT shows fluid around pancreas without a defined wall

complications.name: Pancreatic pseudocyst
clues: Persistent pain or fullness weeks after onset
CT shows a well-defined cystic lesion after 4 weeks

complications.name: Walled-off pancreatic necrosis
clues: Necrotic collection on CT after 4 weeks

special_populations.differences: Less common; causes include trauma, hereditary pancreatitis, and systemic disease. May present with vague abdominal pain and vomiting; ultrasound first.
Gallstone pancreatitis is more common; pain and fever may be absent, and confusion or hypotension may be the presenting feature. Higher mortality from comorbidity.
Gallstones are the most common cause. Use ultrasound and MRCP; avoid CT unless severe. ERCP can be done with fetal protection if cholangitis is present.
Higher risk of severe pancreatitis, necrosis, and organ failure; may require earlier ICU monitoring and attention to metabolic derangements.
Hyperglycemia may be more severe due to pancreatic endocrine dysfunction; glucose control is important, and DKA-like presentations can occur.

key_questions.question: When did the pain start?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over one to two hours, often after a large meal or alcohol binge

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and does it go anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Epigastric or left upper quadrant pain radiating straight through to the back

key_questions.question: How severe is the pain on a 0–10 scale, and what does it feel like?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe, constant, boring pain, often 8–10 out of 10

key_questions.question: What makes the pain better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worsened by lying flat, eating, or deep breathing; improved by leaning forward

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea and vomiting, usually after the pain started

key_questions.question: Have you been able to eat or drink anything?
key_questions.looking_for: Loss of appetite and avoidance of food because it worsens pain

key_questions.question: Have you had fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade fever; high fever with rigors suggests cholangitis

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and has there been a recent binge?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy alcohol use or binge as a cause

key_questions.question: Do you have gallstones or a history of gallbladder problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Gallstone pancreatitis, the most common cause

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including any new or over-the-counter drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Drugs associated with pancreatitis such as azathioprine, valproic acid, mercaptopurine, mesalamine, or didanosine

key_questions.question: Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy itself or ectopic pregnancy; affects imaging choice

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had pancreatitis or very high triglycerides?
Do you have a history of high triglycerides or high calcium?
Have you had any recent procedures, especially an ERCP, or any abdominal trauma?
Are you having any chest pain or shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Alternative diagnosis such as myocardial infarction or respiratory complication from severe pancreatitis

reasoning_points: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, constant and boring in quality
Nausea and vomiting that begin after the pain, with anorexia
Risk factors present such as gallstones or heavy alcohol use
Serum lipase elevated to at least three times the upper limit of normal, or characteristic CT findings
Revised Atlanta criteria: two of three of typical pain, elevated lipase/amylase, and imaging consistent with pancreatitis
Exclusion of important mimics: negative pregnancy test, no free intraperitoneal air, no ST-segment elevation, no evidence of cholangitis
Assessment of severity using BISAP or Atlanta criteria, with attention to volume status and organ failure

easy: Young adult with an alcohol binge and classic epigastric pain radiating to the back
Lipase over 1000 U/L and mild epigastric tenderness only
Ultrasound shows gallstones or a normal biliary tree
No organ failure or significant comorbidity
medium: Older woman with gallstones but less dramatic pain and mild jaundice
Pregnancy with gallstone pancreatitis requiring ultrasound and MRCP instead of CT
Hypertriglyceridemia as the cause, with a lipemic blood sample
Moderate severity with transient hypotension or mild acute kidney injury
hard: Severe necrotizing pancreatitis with persistent organ failure, hypotension, and hypocalcemia
Post-ERCP pancreatitis in a patient who cannot report pain clearly
Child with vague abdominal pain and vomiting, where pancreatitis is not initially suspected
Older adult with confusion and hypotension but only mild epigastric pain and a normal white count
